To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) resident species that have relatively large potential body size have generally lower density (i.e., lower local abundance) and (2) there is a general positive relationship between potential body size and the minimum reproductive threshold size across species.

(1) resident species body size distribution is generally strongly right-skewed; (2) resident species with larger maximum potential body sizes generally have a larger minimum threshold size (MIN); (3) resident species with a smaller MIN generally have greater local recruitment success and hence greater local abundance/densities (including density of reproductive individuals); and (4) resident species with smaller MIN have a greater ability to recruit offspring that survive and reproduce despite intense and persistent competition from near neighbors.

(1) resident species that have relatively large maximum potential body size generally have relatively small minimum reproductive size, and hence relatively small minimum reproductive body size; (2) local density is generally greater for species that have relatively small minimum (and hence relatively small maximum) potential body size; and (3) local density is also generally greater for species – relative to other resident species – that have a relatively large minimum (and hence a relatively small maximum) reproductive threshold size
